label: prop:Delta-system
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Delta-system} Let $n\in\omega$, and let $\mathscr{A}$ be an infinite family of sets such that $|M|\le 
n$ for all $M\in \mathscr{A}$. Then there exist a set $R$ and an infinite family $\mathscr{B}\subset \mathscr{A}$ 
of sets of the same cardinality such that $A\cap B=R$ for any distinct $A,B\in \mathscr{B}$. Moreover, 
$A\setminus R\neq\varnothing$ for all $A\in\mathscr{B}$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
We say that a topological space $X$ is {\it strongly $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn} if, given any $x\in X$ and 
any decreasing sequence $(U_n)_{n\in \omega}$ of open subsets of $X$ for which $x\in \bigcap_{n\in \omega} 
\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U_n$, there exists a sequence $(x_n)_{n \in\omega}$ converging to $x$ such that $x_n \in  U_n$ for all 
$n \in \omega$.
head: environment

label: p1
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(ii):\enspace
For each $n\in\omega$, let $W_n=\bigcup_{k\ge n} U_k$. The sets $W_n$ are open and decreasing, and 
$x\in\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{W}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}W_n$ for all $n$.
It follows from (i) that there is a sequence $(y_n)_{n \in\omega}$ converging to $x$ 
and such that $y_n \in W_n$ for all $n \in \omega$, i.e., $y_n\in U_{m_n}$ for some $m_n\geq n$. 
Since $m_n\to\infty$, we can choose indices $j_0<j_1<\dots$ so that $m_{j_0}<m_{j_1}<\dots$\,. 
It remains to set $x_k=y_{j_k}$ and $n_k=m_{j_k}$.

(ii)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(i):\enspace 
Let $x\in X$, and let $(U_n)_{n\in \omega}$ be a decreasing sequence of open subsets in $X$ for which $x\in 
\bigcap_{n\in \omega} \stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U_n$. By (ii) there exist a sequence $(x_k)_{k\in\omega}$ converging to $x$ and 
a strictly increasing sequence $(n_k)_{k\in\omega}$ such that $x_k\in U_{n_k}$. Since $n_k\geq k$ and 
the sequence $(U_n)$ decreases, we have $x_k\in U_k$ for all $k\in\omega$.
head: environment

label: p2
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(ii)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(i):\enspace 
In view of Proposition~\ref{p1}, it suffices to show that if $x\in X$ and $(U_n)_{n\in\omega}$ is a sequence of 
open subsets in $X$ for which $x\in \bigcap_{n\in \omega} \stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U_n$, then condition~(ii) of 
Proposition~\ref{p1} holds. We set $U=\bigcup_{n\in\omega}U_n\times \{n\}$. Then $U$ is open and $(x,\omega)\in 
\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U$. From (ii) it follows that there exists a sequence $\bigl((y_j,m_j)\bigr)_{j\in \omega}\subset U$ 
converging to $(x,\omega)$; thus, $y_j\in U_{m_j}$, $y_j\to x$, and $m_j\to\infty$. Passing to a subsequence, we 
can assume that the $m_j$ strictly increase, as required. 

(iii)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(i):\enspace 
The proof is similar to that of (ii)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(i). Let $x\in X$, and let $(U_n)_{n\in\omega}$ be a sequence of 
open subsets of $X$ for which $x\in\bigcap_{n\in\omega}\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U_n$. We set 
$U=\bigcup_{n\in\omega}U_n\times\bigl(\frac1{n+2},\frac1{n+1}\bigr)$. Then $U$ is open in $X\times[0,1]$ and 
$(x,0)\in\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U$. By (iii) there exists a sequence $\bigl((y_j,t_j)\bigr)_{j\in\omega}\subset U$ converging to 
$(x,0)$. Let $m_j$ be such that $(y_j,t_j)\in U_{m_j}\times\bigl(\frac1{m_j+2},\frac1{m_j+1}\bigr)$. Then $y_j\in U_{m_j}$, 
$y_j\to x$, and $m_j\to\infty$, because $t_j\to0$. Passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the $m_j$ 
strictly increase, so that condition~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{p1} holds. 

(i)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(iv):\enspace 
Take $(x,y)\in X\times Y$ and an open subset $U$ of $X\times Y$ for which $(x,y)\in \stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U$.
Let $\{V_n:n\in\omega\}$ be a decreasing countable base of open neighborhoods of $y$, and let 
\begin{align*}
\pi_X &\colon X\times Y \to X,\ (x,y)\mapsto x,
\\
\pi_Y &\colon X\times Y \to Y,\ (x,y)\mapsto y
\end{align*}
be the projections. We set $U_n=\pi_X(U\cap \pi^{-1}_Y(V_n))$ for $n\in\omega$. Then $x\in \stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U_n$ and 
$U_{n+1}\subset U_n$ for $n\in\omega$. From (i) it follows that there exists a sequence $(x_n)_{n \in \omega}$ 
converging to $x$ and such that $x_n \in U_n$ for all $n \in \omega$. For each $n \in \omega$, choose a $y_n \in 
V_n$ such that $(x_n,y_n) \in U$. The sequence $\bigl((x_n,y_n)\bigr)_{n \in \omega}$ converges to $(x,y)$.

The implications (iv)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(ii), (iv)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(iii), and (v)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(iv) are obvious. 

It remains to prove that (iv)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(v). Let $Y$ be a first-countable space. Then $Y\times 
(\omega+1)$ is first-countable and (iv) implies that $X\times Y\times (\omega+1)$ is 
$\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn. Since (ii)\,$\Rightarrow$\,(i), it follows that $X\times Y$ is strongly 
$\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn.
head: environment

label: t1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t1}
Any $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn group is strongly $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}\-chet--Ury\-sohn.
head: environment

label: rem:finer
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:finer}
If $X$ is a topological space with topology $\tau$, $\tau'$ is another topology on $X$ finer than $\tau$, and a 
family $\mathscr F$ of subsets of $X$ absorbs convergent sequences in $(X,\tau)$, then $\mathscr F$ absorbs 
convergent sequences in $(X, \tau')$. Similarly, if $\mathscr F$ absorbs convergent sequences in $X$ and 
$Y\subset X$, then $\{F\cap Y:F\in\mathscr F\}$ absorbs convergent sequences in~$Y$.
head: environment

label: lemma:ind-limit
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that a sequence $(x_k)_{k\in\omega}$ converges to $x\in Z$ but is contained in no $K_n$. 
Any finite subset of $Z$ is contained in some $K_n$, because the $K_n$ increase and cover $Z$. Hence, for each 
$j\in\omega$ and each $p\in \omega$, there exists a $k>p$ such that $x_k\notin K_j$. This allows us to choose 
indices $k_0<k_1<\dots$ so that $x_{k_j}\notin K_j$ for all $j$. Let $m\in\omega$ be such that $x\in K_m$, 
and let $A=\{x_{k_j}:j\geq m\}$. Then $x\notin A$, because $x_{k_j}\notin K_j\supset K_m$ for $j\geq m$, and 
$x\in \stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{A}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}A$, because $x_{k_j}\to x$. On the other hand, $A\cap K_n\subset\{x_{k_j}:j<n\}$ is finite and hence 
closed in $K_n$ for each $n$; therefore, $A$ is closed in $Z$. This contradiction proves the lemma.
head: environment

label: p3
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i)\enspace 
Suppose that, on the contrary, $Y=X\setminus \stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{\bigcup_{n\in\omega}\operatorname{Int} F_n}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}\bigcup_{n\in\omega}\operatorname{Int} F_n\neq\varnothing$. Note that 
$Y$ is open. No point $y\in Y$ is isolated in $Y$: otherwise, $\{y\}$ is open in $X$, and since $y\in F_n$ for 
some $n$, we have $y\in \operatorname{Int} F_n$. Take $y\in Y$. The set $Y\setminus\{y\}$ is open and $y\in 
\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{Y\setminus\{y\}}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}Y\setminus\{y\}$. Since $X$ is $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn, there exists a sequence $(y_n)_{n\in 
\omega}\subset Y\setminus\{y\}$ converging to $y$. For each $n\in\omega$, choose an open set $U_n$ so that 
$y_n\in U_n\subset Y$ and $y\notin \stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U_n$. We set $V_n=U_n\setminus F_n$ and $V=\bigcup_{n\in\omega}V_n$. 
The open set $U_n$ does not meet $\operatorname{Int} F_n$; hence $V_n$ is dense in $U_n$ and $y_n\in \stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{V}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}V_n$. Since 
$y_n\to y$, it follows that $y\in\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{V}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}V$, and since $X$ is $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn, there exists a 
sequence $(x_k)_{k\in \omega}$, $x_k\in V$, converging to~$y$.

Let us show that $\{x_k:k\in\omega\}\not\subset F_m$ for every $m\in\omega$; this will contradict the assumption 
that $\mathscr F$ absorbs convergent sequences. Since $y\notin\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{U_0\cup\dots\cup U_m}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}U_0\cup\dots\cup U_m$, only finitely 
many $x_k$ belong to $U_0\cup\dots\cup U_m$. Take $k$ with $x_k\notin U_0\cup\dots\cup U_m$. Then $x_k\in V_j$ 
for some $j>m$, so that $x_k\notin F_j\supset F_m$.

(ii)\enspace 
Assume that, on the contrary, $Y=X\setminus \bigcup_{n\in\omega}\operatorname{Int} F_n\neq\varnothing$. Take $y\in Y$. Let 
$V_n=X\setminus F_n$ for $n\in \omega$. The open sets $V_n$ decrease, and $y\in \stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{V}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}V_n$, because $y\notin 
\operatorname{Int} F_n$. Since $X$ is strongly $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn, there exists a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\omega}$ 
converging to $y$ and such that $x_n\in V_n$, i.e., $x_n\notin F_n$, for $n\in \omega$. The sequence $(x_n)_{n\in 
\omega}$ is not contained in any $F_n$, which contradicts the assumption that $\mathscr F$ absorbs convergent 
sequences.
head: environment

label: c1
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Replacing $K_n$ by $K_0\cup\dots\cup K_n$, we can assume that the $K_n$ increase. The family $\{K_n:n\in\omega\}$ 
absorbs convergent sequences, because any convergent sequence together with its limit is compact. It remains to 
apply Proposition~\ref{p3} and note that every point of $\operatorname{Int} K_n$ has the compact neighborhood $K_n$.
head: environment

label: c2
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{c2}
Any hemicompact homogeneous $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn \tolerance1500 space $X$ is locally compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Corollary~\ref{c1}(i), $X$ has a point of local compactness, and by homogeneity all points of $X$ are points 
of local compactness.
head: environment

label: prop:kfu-group-as
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:kfu-group-as}
Suppose that a family $\mathscr F=\{F_n: n\in \omega\}$ of closed subsets of a $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn 
topological group $G$ absorbs convergent sequences in~$G$ and $F_n\subset F_{n+1}$ for all $n\in\omega$. Then 
$F_n$ is a neighborhood of the identity element of $G$ for some $n \in \omega$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
According to Theorem~\ref{t1}, $G$ is strongly $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn. \tolerance1000
Therefore, $\bigcup_{n\in\omega}\operatorname{Int} F_n=G$ by Proposition~\ref{p3}(ii); in particular, the identity 
element belongs to some $\operatorname{Int} F_n$.
head: environment

label: prop:kfu-group-loc-precomp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:kfu-group-loc-precomp}
Suppose that a family $\mathscr F=\{F_n: n\in \omega\}$ of closed precompact subsets of a topological group $G$ 
absorbs convergent sequences in~$G$. Then any $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn subgroup of $G$ is locally 
precompact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H$ be a $\varkappa$-Fr\'{e}chet--Urysohn subgroup of $G$, and let $P_n = (F_0\cup\dots\cup F_n) \cap H$ for 
$n \in \omega$. Then the increasing family $\mathscr{P} = \{P_n : n \in \omega\}$ consists of closed subsets of 
$H$ precompact in $G$ and hence in $H$, and $\mathscr{P}$ absorbs convergent sequences in $H$ (see 
Remark~\ref{rem:finer}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:kfu-group-as} one of the precompact sets $P_n$ is a 
neighborhood of the identity element of $H$. Therefore, $H$ is locally precompact.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Given a variety $\mathscr{V}$, a set $X$, and $g\in F^\mathscr{V}(X)$, we put  
$$
\operatorname{supp} g=\bigcap \{A\subset X: g\in \langle A\rangle\}. 
$$
We refer to $\operatorname{supp} g$ as the \emph{support} of $g$ in~$F^\mathscr{V}(X)$.
head: environment

label: prop:property_afg
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: lemma:afg-intersection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:afg-intersection}
If ${\mathscr{V}}$ is a variety of abstract groups, $X$ a nonempty set, and $F^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$ 
the free group on $X$ in $\mathscr{V}$, then 
$\langle A\rangle \cap \langle B\rangle =\langle A\cap B\rangle$ for any $A,B\subset X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to check that $\langle A\rangle \cap \langle B\rangle \subset \langle A\cap B\rangle$. Take 
$g\in \langle A\rangle \cap \langle B\rangle$; we have $g = 
a_1^{\varepsilon_1}\dots a_n^{\varepsilon_n}$, where $n\in \omega$, $a_i\in A$, 
$\varepsilon_i\in \{-1,1\}$ for $i\le n$.
Let $f\colon X\to F^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$ be the map defined by setting $f(x)=x$ for $x\in B$ and $f(x)=e$ 
for $x\notin B$, and let $\hat f\colon F^\mathscr{V}(X)\to F^\mathscr{V}(X)$ be the extension of $f$ to a homomorphism. 
Since $g\in \langle B\rangle$, we have $\hat f(g)=g$. 
Let us number the indices $k\le n$ for which $a_k\in B$ in increasing order: 
$$
\{k\in\{1,\dots,n\}: a_k\in B\}=\{k_1,\dots,k_m\}.
$$
Then
\[
g=\hat f(g)=f(a_1)^{\varepsilon_1}f(a_2)^{\varepsilon_2}\dots f(a_n)^{\varepsilon_n}=a_{k_1}^{\varepsilon_{k_1}}\dots a_{k_m}^{\varepsilon_{k_m}},
\]
where all $a_{k_i}$ belong to $A\cap B$. Therefore, $g\in \langle A\cap B\rangle$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The case where $g$ is the identity element of $F^\mathscr{V}(X)$ is trivial. In what follows, we assume that 
$g\ne e$. 

Let $n$ be the length of $g$ in $F^\mathscr{V}(X)$. Then $g=x_1^{\varepsilon_1}x_2^{\varepsilon_2}\dots x_n^{\varepsilon_n}$ 
for some $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$ and $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n\in \{-1,1\}$.
We set $\mathscr{A}=\{A\subset X: g\in \langle A\rangle\}$ and $S=\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$. Then $S\in \mathscr{A}$ and $|S|\leq n$.

(i)\enspace
According to Lemma~\ref{lemma:afg-intersection}, the family $\mathscr{A}$ is closed under finite intersections. 
Let $\mathscr{A}'=\{A\cap S: A\in \mathscr{A}\}$. 
As mentioned, $S\in \mathscr{A}$; consequently, $\mathscr{A}'\subset \mathscr{A}$ and $\operatorname{supp} g=\bigcap \mathscr{A}'$. 
Since the family $\mathscr{A}'$ is finite (because so is $S$) 
and $\mathscr{A}$ is closed under finite intersections, we have $\operatorname{supp} g\in \mathscr{A}$, that is, $g\in \langle \operatorname{supp} g\rangle$.

Assertion (ii) follows from the definition of $\operatorname{supp} g$.

(iii)\enspace
We must show that $\operatorname{supp} g=S$. Clearly, $\operatorname{supp} g\subset S$. 
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:afg-intersection}, we 
number the indices $k\le n$ for which $x_k\in \operatorname{supp} g$ in increasing order: 
$$
\{k\in \{1,\dots,n\}: x_k\in \operatorname{supp} g\}=\{k_1,\dots,k_m\}.
$$
Note that $\operatorname{supp} g\ne S$ if and only if $m<n$.  
Let $f\colon X\to F^\mathscr{V}(X)$ be the map defined by setting $f(x)=x$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp} g$ and $f(x)=e$ 
for $x\notin\operatorname{supp} g$, and let $\hat f\colon F^\mathscr{V}(X)\to F^\mathscr{V}(X)$ be the extension of $f$ to a homomorphism. 
Since $g\in \langle \operatorname{supp} g\rangle$, we have $\hat f(g)=g$. Applying $\hat f$ to 
$g=x_1^{\varepsilon_1}\dots x_n^{\varepsilon_n}$, we obtain the product 
$$
f(x_1)^{\varepsilon_1}f(x_2)^{\varepsilon_2}\dots f(x_n)^{\varepsilon_n} = x_{k_1}^{\varepsilon_{k_1}}\dots x_{k_m}^{\varepsilon_{k_m}}.
$$ 
If $m<n$, then the length of $g$ is strictly less than $n$, which contradicts our assumption. Therefore, 
$m=n$ and $\operatorname{supp} g= S$.
head: environment

label: rem:supp
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:supp}
The support of an element $g$ in a free, free Abelian, or free Boolean group is simply the set of letters of the 
reduced word representing~$g$. The definition of $\operatorname{supp} g$ for an arbitrary variety of groups and its properties 
established in Lemma~\ref{lemma:afg-intersection} and Proposition~\ref{prop:property_afg} are very natural and 
may be folklore. The notion of support is closely related to that of an essential variable for an element of 
a universal algebra (see, e.g.,~\cite{Salomaa}).
head: environment

label: prop:afgk
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i)\enspace
Clearly, $F_k^{\mathscr{V}}(A)\subset \langle A\rangle \cap F_k^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$. 
Let us prove the reverse inclusion. Let $g\in \langle A\rangle \cap F_k^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$, and let 
$n$ be the length of $g$ in $F^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$. Then $n\leq k$.
It follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:property_afg}(ii) that $\operatorname{supp} g\subset A$.
Let $g=x_1^{\varepsilon_1}\dots x_n^{\varepsilon_n}$ be a representation of $g$ by a word of length $n$. By 
Proposition~\ref{prop:property_afg}(iii), $\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}=\operatorname{supp} g\subset A$; thus, this is a word in $A$, 
and the length of $g$ in $F^{\mathscr{V}}(A)$ does not exceed~$n$.
Therefore, $g\in F_k^{\mathscr{V}}(A)$.

(ii)\enspace 
The set $F_k^{\mathscr{V}}(A)$ is obviously finite for finite~$A$.
head: environment

label: prop:afgn-finete
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $g\in F^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$, let $l(g)$ denote the length of $g$ in $F^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$. By 
Proposition~\ref{prop:property_afg}(iii), $|\operatorname{supp} g|\le l(g)$; by Proposition~\ref{prop:property_afg}(i) 
and~(ii), $\operatorname{supp}(gh)\subset\operatorname{supp} g\cup\operatorname{supp} h$ and $\operatorname{supp} g^{-1}=\operatorname{supp} g$ for $g,h\in F^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$.
Consider two cases.

First, suppose that the set $\{l(g): g\in M\}$ is unbounded. Let $g\in M$. Choose an $h\in M$ so that $l(h)> n 
l(g) + n$. Since $h=h g^n g^{-n}$ and $n l(g) + n<l(h)\leq l(h g^n) + l(g^{-n})\leq l(h g^n) + n l(g)$, we have 
$l(h g^n)>n$, that is, $h g^n\notin F_n^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$. It remains to note that $h g^n\in M^{n+1}$.

Now suppose that the set $\{l(g): g\in M\}$ is bounded, that is, $M\subset F_k^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$ for some $k\in 
\omega$. Let $U=\bigcup\{\operatorname{supp} g: g\in M\}$. Proposition \ref{prop:property_afg}(i) implies the inclusion 
$M\subset \langle U\rangle$. Since $M$ is infinite and $M\subset \langle U\rangle\cap F_k^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$, it 
follows that $\langle U\rangle\cap F_k^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$ is infinite. By Proposition~\ref{prop:afgk}(ii) the set 
$U$ is infinite. Therefore, so is the family $\{\operatorname{supp} g: g\in M\}$. Since $|\operatorname{supp} g|\le l(g)\le k$ for every 
$g\in M$, Proposition~\ref{prop:Delta-system} implies the existence of a finite set $D\subset X$ and elements 
$g_m\in M$, $m\in\omega$, with pairwise distinct supports such that $\operatorname{supp} g_i\cap \operatorname{supp} g_j=D$ for any distinct 
$i,j\in\omega$ and $\operatorname{supp} g_i\setminus D\ne\varnothing$ for all $i$. Let \[ g=g_0 g_1\dots g_n. \] Then $g\in 
M^{n+1}$.

Let us show that $g\notin F_n^{\mathscr{V}}(X)$. In view of Proposition~\ref{prop:property_afg}(iii), it suffices 
to prove that $|\operatorname{supp} g|>n$. For each $i=0,1,\dots,n$, take an $x_i\in \operatorname{supp} g_i\setminus D$. We claim that $x_i 
\in \operatorname{supp} g$ for every $i=0,1,\dots,n$. Indeed, note that $x_i\notin \operatorname{supp} g_j$ for $j\neq i$. We have $g=p g_i 
q$, where $p=g_0 g_1\dots g_{i-1}$ and $q=g_{i+1}\dots g_{n}$. Since $\operatorname{supp} p\subset \bigcup_{j=0}^{i-1}\operatorname{supp} 
g_j$ and $\operatorname{supp} q\subset \bigcup_{j=i+1}^{n}\operatorname{supp} g_j$, it follows that $x_i\notin \operatorname{supp} p$ and $x_i\notin \operatorname{supp} 
q$. We have 
$$
x_i\in\operatorname{supp} g_i= \operatorname{supp} (p^{-1} g q^{-1}) \subset \operatorname{supp} p \cup \operatorname{supp} g \cup \operatorname{supp} q
$$
and $x_i\notin \operatorname{supp} p\cup \operatorname{supp} q$; therefore, $x_i\in\operatorname{supp} g$.

Since $x_i\neq x_j$ for different $i$ and $j$, it follows that $|\operatorname{supp} g|>n$.
head: environment

label: new_old_theorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{new_old_theorem}
For any full variety $\mathscr V$ of topological groups and any Tychonoff space $X$, all sets 
$F_n^\mathscr{V}(X)$, $n\in \omega$, are closed in $F^\mathscr{V}(X)$ and the family $\{F_n^\mathscr{V}(X): n\in 
\omega\}$ absorbs convergent sequences in $F^\mathscr{V}(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $K$ be any compact space containing $X$ (e.g., $K=\beta X$). The embedding of $X$ into $K$ extends to a 
continuous homomorphism $i\colon F^\mathscr{V}(X)\to F^\mathscr{V}(K)$; its image is the subgroup $\langle  
X\rangle$ of $F^\mathscr{V}(K)$, which is algebraically the free group $F^{\hbox{\scriptsize$ 
  \setbox0=\hbox{$\skew3\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{\mathscr{V}}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}\mathscr{V}$} 
  \ht0=\dimexpr\ht0-.15ex\relax 
  \skew3\stackengine{0pt}{}{\overline{\phantom{\copy0}}}{O}{l}{F}{T}{L}\copy0$}}(X)$ (see 
Section~\ref{sec:free_abstract_groups}), and hence $i$ is injective. We identify $F^\mathscr{V}(X)$ with $\langle 
X\rangle\subset F^\mathscr{V}(K)$ as an abstract group; the topology of $F^\mathscr{V}(X)$ is finer than that 
inherited from $F^\mathscr{V}(K)$, and $F_n^\mathscr{V}(X)=F_n^\mathscr{V}(K)\cap F^\mathscr{V}(X)$ by 
Proposition~\ref{prop:afgk}(i).

Mal'tsev proved that $F^\mathscr{V}(K)$ has the inductive limit topology with respect to the decomposition 
$F^\mathscr{V}(K)= \bigcup_{n\in \omega}F_n^\mathscr{V}(K)$ \cite[Lemma in Section~5]{Maltsev1957}. 
Each set $F_n^\mathscr{V}(K)$ is compact, being the image of the compact space 
$\bigl(K\oplus \{e\}\oplus K^{-1}\bigr)^n$ under the continuous natural multiplication map 
$(x_1,\dots, x_n)\mapsto x_1\dots x_n$. Therefore, each $F_n^\mathscr{V}(K)$ is closed in $F^\mathscr{V}(K)$ and 
hence each $F_n^\mathscr{V}(X)$ is closed in $F^\mathscr{V}(X)$.

By Lemma~\ref{lemma:ind-limit} the family $\{F_n^\mathscr{V}(K): n\in\omega\}$ absorbs convergent sequences in 
$F^\mathscr{V}(K)$. By Remark~\ref{rem:finer} the family $\{F_n^\mathscr{V}(K)\cap F^\mathscr{V}(X): 
n\in\omega\}=\{F_n^\mathscr{V}(X): n\in \omega\}$ absorbs convergent sequences in $F^\mathscr{V}(X)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $e$ be the identity element of $F^\mathscr{V}(X)$. By Theorem~\ref{new_old_theorem} 
each $F_n^\mathscr{V}(X)$ is closed in 
$F^\mathscr{V}(X)$; therefore, each $F_n^\mathscr{V}(X)\cap G$ is closed in $G$. 
Suppose that there exists a $k$ for which $F_k^\mathscr{V}(X)\cap G$ has nonempty 
interior in $G$, i.e., contains a neighborhood $U$ of some word $g\in F_k^\mathscr{V}(X)\cap G$. 
Then, for some neighborhood $V$ of $e$ in $G$, we have $gV\subset U$. Clearly, 
$V\subset g^{-1}U\subset F_{2k}^\mathscr{V}(X)$. 
Let $W$ be a neighborhood  of $e$ in $G$ for which $W^{2k+1}\subset V$.
Since $G$ is a nondiscrete Hausdorff group, the set $W$ is infinite.
Proposition~\ref{prop:afgn-finete} implies $W^{2k+1}\not\subset F_{2k}^\mathscr{V}(X)$. This  contradiction 
proves Proposition~\ref{new_old_proposition}.
